questions.q: Why does this lesson describe adding an index without measuring first as "guessing"?
options: Without a baseline measurement, you can't verify the change helped, and an added index can slow down writes even as it speeds up reads
MySQL indexes never actually improve query performance
Indexes can only be added by a database administrator with root access
Measuring is only necessary for physical backups, not for indexing
questions.explain: An unmeasured change can't be verified, and it might trade a bigger problem (slower writes) for a smaller one, unnoticed.

questions.q: What are the four steps of the tuning loop described in this lesson, in order?
options: Measure, identify, change, verify
Change, measure, guess, verify
Identify, change, measure, guess
Verify, change, identify, measure
questions.explain: The loop is measure what's happening, identify the specific bottleneck, make one targeted change, then verify it helped.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist on making one targeted change at a time rather than several at once?
options: Making multiple changes at once makes it impossible to know which one actually caused any improvement
MySQL only allows one configuration change per session
Multiple changes always cancel each other out
One change at a time is a MySQL licensing requirement
questions.explain: A scattershot set of changes prevents isolating which change was actually responsible for any measured improvement.

questions.q: Which MySQL tool does this lesson identify as the most direct way to find which queries are actually slow?
options: The slow query log
SHOW CREATE TABLE
mysqldump
The InnoDB buffer pool size setting
questions.explain: The slow query log records queries exceeding a configured execution time threshold, directly surfacing what's actually slow.

questions.q: How does this lesson characterize MySQL's performance tuning loop compared to SQL Server's?
options: Identical in shape (measure, identify, change, verify) but different in the specific instrumentation tools used
Completely unrelated methodologies with nothing in common
MySQL has no performance tuning methodology at all
SQL Server's methodology doesn't apply to any other database platform
questions.explain: The discipline transfers directly from SQL Server; what differs is the real MySQL tooling (slow query log, EXPLAIN, Performance Schema, sys schema) plugged into that same loop.
